DOSSIER

### ASSESSMENT
The country criminalises no conduct on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex acts have been legal since the Supreme Court's December 2007 judgment in Sunil Babu Pant v. the national government, which held that homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The Criminal Codes Act 2017, which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still lists 'unnatural sex' on its face and must be read in light of that ruling; the Muluki Ain criminalised 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and many LGBTQI+ people were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition rests on the 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognising the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration. Government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while changes to 'male' or 'female' markers lagged, so the progressive reputation outruns policy. A human-rights organisation called in February 2024 on the government to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure for transgender and third-gender people to obtain official documents, indicating no straightforward document-change process exists; a trans woman photographed that month held a 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender. In a decision publicly reported in July 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that a trans law student must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed more than 50 lawsuits beginning in 2021. The decision orders recognition for her alone: others must still petition the court, and the typical medical and surgical requirements persisted for them. Before that ruling, changing markers to 'female' or 'male' had usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. Local activists assessed in September 2020 that an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. Marriage and partnership recognition is partial. Judicial recognition of foreign same-sex marriages exists: a Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas. On 28 June 2023 a Supreme Court justice issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the national identity and civil registration department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration grants no equal rights: such couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 a national LGBT organisation counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: a district court rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown. Ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities were reported in November 2024 from a city in the southern plains: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. A 2015 academic study found that despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life. Gender-affirming care is limited. The first gender-affirming surgery in the country was performed in June 2025 at a national university teaching hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 rupees, providers are few, and many trans residents take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma. Some travel to a neighbouring jurisdiction and to a jurisdiction in the region for surgery. Conversion therapy is practiced, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members. Lesbian couples are denied IVF, and research and healthcare addressing LGBT residents' needs are severely lacking. A drop-in centre with free HIV testing operates in the capital through a national LGBT organisation with more than 50 branches; three other community organisations also provide resources. The national development programme has recommended that transgender and intersex students be given access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities. Hostility has surfaced alongside the protective framework, though the documented instances are not official government acts: a non-governing political party's protest rally, the elected head of government's reported personal video, and threats made by that leader's supporters. On 30 October 2024 a political party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, with a community organisation's executive director noting that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in the country and the subregion. In April 2026 the newly elected head of government faced LGBTQ community criticism over a video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community. A former governing party made homophobic statements during the Civil War, describing homosexuality as 'a production of capitalism' and LGBT people as 'social pollutants'. A 2008 international newspaper report quotes the 'social pollutants' wording as the former rebels' past description of gays and lesbians, and also records that a political party and the party of the former rebels wrote support for gay rights into their platforms — a historical 2008 party-platform change that does not establish the parties' present-day stance and concerned gay rights rather than trans-specific rights. Education and civic space: the national education board has implemented information about sexual and gender diversity in the curriculum for grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), making the country the second in the region to do so, and universities offer courses on LGBT issues. Many LGBT children nonetheless face discrimination and leave school because of threats, bullying and neglect by fellow students and teachers, and transgender residents face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, especially in rural areas. A national queer youth organisation has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and has advocated for the citizenship bill. During the 2011 census, some enumerators demanded that a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender'. Pride events held annually include a national pride parade (since 2019), a queer womxn pride and a trans pride parade (since 2020).

### SOURCE EVIDENCE
- An international observer's report (February 2024) calls on the government to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents, illustrating that despite progressive rulings no straightforward document-change process exists.
- An international human-rights report (31 July 2024) records the supreme court's decision that a trans law student must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification; the order applies to her alone, while others must still petition the court and the typical medical and surgical requirements for marker changes persisted for others.
- A news report (August 2024) records that the supreme court ruled a trans woman must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed many lawsuits; previously, changing markers usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations.
- A news analysis (February 2024) argues that the 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but officials limited changes to people identifying as third-gender while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns its policy.
- A news feature (November 2024) records ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities: discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions, and frequent physical and sexual harassment.
- A community publication (October 2021) records a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition.
- A contributor analysis (September 2020) argues that despite the constitutional right to self-determine name and gender markers, an extensive overhaul of the law is still needed to address inequalities.
- A study-abroad paper (2015) records that despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in nearly every arena of life.
- A news report (2 May 2008) records that a political party and the party of the former rebels, whose leaders had previously described gays and lesbians as social 'pollutants', wrote support for gay rights into their platforms — a historical 2008 party-platform change, not evidence of every later policy, and a gay-rights rather than trans-specific commitment.

### SECONDARY / SITUATIONAL FACTORS
Media representation of LGBT people has historically been negative or comic relief, with caricatures of transgender people, gay people and lesbians, though positive depictions include two films released in 2012. Some observers accused media and activists of pinkwashing and spreading disinformation about same-sex marriage and LGBT rights, and national media has been criticised for forcefully using 'third gender' to describe trans men and trans women. The country's progressive international reputation rests on the 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender, which was novel at the time and later reinforced by subsequent cases; the gap between that doctrine and implementation is documented by a February 2024 analysis and by a February 2024 call from a human-rights organisation for a clear document-change procedure.

### AFFECTS RESIDENTS MORE THAN VISITORS
Residents' access to legal gender recognition improved with the Supreme Court's decision, publicly reported in July 2024, that a trans woman be recognised on all documents without medical verification. The ruling applies to her alone: other residents must still petition the court for a 'male'/'female' marker change, where surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including post-operative genital exams remained the usual requirements. Third-gender marker changes by self-declaration had been available earlier, but officials limited changes to that category. Same-sex couples may register marriages under the 28 June 2023 interim order and the April 2024 instruction to enter them in a separate register, but the registration carries no equal rights: no inheritance, no tax subsidies, no spousal medical decision-making, no adoption, and certificates read 'groom and bride'. Compliance by local governments is unknown and a district court rejected a registration in July 2023. A national queer youth organisation has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and has advocated for the citizenship bill. Civil society produced a Gender Identity Draft Bill in October 2021 through a regional transgender network's fellowship, authored by two activists with a legal advocate. Local activists assessed in September 2020 that an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law is still needed. Healthcare and support infrastructure: a national university teaching hospital performed the country's first gender-affirming surgery in June 2025 and has established a Gender Affirming Clinic; hormone therapy remains costly (4,500 rupees for a six-month supply) and providers are few, with some residents travelling abroad for surgery. A national LGBT organisation operates a capital-city drop-in centre with free HIV testing and more than 50 branches; three other community organisations also provide resources. Conversion therapy, including rehabilitation-centre treatment and family-organised traditional exorcism, is practiced. Lesbian couples are denied IVF. Education: the national education board has implemented sexual and gender diversity content in grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), and universities offer courses on LGBT issues. LGBT children nonetheless face discrimination, bullying and neglect leading to school dropout, and transgender residents face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, especially in rural areas. The national development programme has recommended safe toilets and bathroom facilities for transgender and intersex students.

### DELIBERATELY NOT COUNTED
The full bench of the Supreme Court has yet to deliver a final verdict on the 28 June 2023 interim order directing temporary registration of same-sex marriages; the outcome is unresolved in this record. Compliance by local governments with the April 2024 instruction to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register is unknown. The 2011 census incident in which some enumerators demanded a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender' is the most recent census-specific episode documented here; no later census episode is sourced. No trans-specific killing rate with a denominator and period is present in this inventory, so no comparative violence magnitude can be stated; the November 2024 account of discrimination and physical and sexual harassment in a provincial city is the most recent ground-level condition documented.

### ASSESSMENT
No criminal provision in the country's law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The legal code derives from the 1889 code of a neighbouring jurisdiction and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender. The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the dominant religious institution and by the country's law. The country has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the country. For a trans visitor, it is unknown whether a trans-specific rule governs access to single-sex facilities, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor. The country operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by the country serves the term in prisons in a neighbouring jurisdiction at the country's expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under the country's authority. A religious education office's 2019 document frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to religious institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity. A 2023 declaration by the doctrinal office permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves. The country has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. The head of the dominant religious institution in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside that institution while maintaining that marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. In 2021 the foreign minister wrote to the ambassador of a neighbouring jurisdiction objecting to a parliamentary bill there meant to protect LGBT people against violence and discrimination. The objection targeted the provision prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which the letter described as a violation of freedom of speech and of religion, and asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated. On 13 January 1998 an activist set himself on fire in a central square, under the country's jurisdiction, in protest at the dominant religion's refusal of homosexuality. He died days later in hospital from severe burns.

### SOURCE EVIDENCE
- The nation operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the nation serve their time in another nation's prisons with costs covered by the nation; there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case. The sole prison-axis source is a general reference article on crime in the nation, used as a last resort.
- The 2024 declaration states that 'any sex-change intervention, as a rule, risks threatening the unique dignity the person has received from the moment of conception', while not excluding medical assistance for genital abnormalities evident at birth or developing later, which in that case would not constitute a sex change in its sense; it condemns 'gender theory' as 'extremely dangerous since it cancels differences' and separately denounces the imprisonment, torture and killing of people solely because of their sexual orientation. The sources report no documented mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; an educational document (2019) opposes 'gender theory' as denying natural difference. The 2024 declaration and the 2019 educational document express institutional doctrine, not rules binding visitors.
- A 2023 declaration permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage, with a January 2024 clarification reiterating that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.
- Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender. The sources cited record no trans-specific practice at entry, at screening, or in access to facilities for a trans visitor, and do not establish what document checks or screening visitors face; neither trans-specific danger nor trans-specific safety can be inferred from them.

### SECONDARY / SITUATIONAL FACTORS
Accreditation rules for foreign diplomats posted to the government bar anyone who is part of a same-sex family and anyone who is divorced. A neighbouring jurisdiction's openly gay nominee, in a civil pact, was rejected in 2008, and an openly gay practising single nominee was rejected in 2015. That jurisdiction left the post vacant from March 2015 until May 2016 before nominating another diplomat. In October 2008 officials of the dominant religious institution rejected that jurisdiction's first-choice candidate as ambassador because he is gay, forcing it to name a different envoy, a documented instance of the government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations. The governing institution's posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy in diplomatic and internal matters, while the country's own criminal law has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct in modern times. The legal baseline of the country and the doctrinal position of the institution that governs it are separate layers.

### AFFECTS RESIDENTS MORE THAN VISITORS
The government reserves the right to remove, suspend or dismiss immediately any official or employee who publicly admits to being gay or who questions the general policy of the government towards homosexuals. The provision applies to people working for the governing institutions rather than to visitors. No anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity applies to residents of the country, and no legal gender recognition procedure exists for them.

### DELIBERATELY NOT COUNTED
No human rights report chapter issued by a national government covers the country for 2023 or 2024, so the assessment rests on encyclopedic and institutional sources rather than a government human rights report. The absence of a documented trans-prisoner placement case reflects the absence of a domestic prison system and of published records, not a finding that no trans person has ever been held in pre-trial detention in the country. Whether the government's stated right to dismiss officials and employees who publicly acknowledge being gay has been exercised in specific cases is not documented in the sources reviewed. Enforcement practice at entry, at screening, or in access to facilities for a trans visitor is not documented. No source records a trans visitor being stopped, questioned or refused entry on grounds of gender identity.

### ASSESSMENT
The Gender Recognition Act 2004, in force since 4 April 2005, allows a transgender person to apply to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate after two years of transition, without mandatory surgery, and to obtain a new birth certificate and legal recognition of acquired gender, subject to statutory exceptions. Certificates continue to be issued. On 16 April 2025, the top court held that 'sex', 'man' and 'woman' in the national equality act refer to biological sex, including for GRC holders; it confirmed that protection from discrimination on the ground of gender reassignment continues. The 2026 regional rainbow-index assessment nevertheless describes the country as having no functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition and limitations making it practically impossible. The ruling affects provisions of the national equality act, including single-sex services; these sources do not establish particular entry or custody rules or how individual visitors will be treated. The framework followed Goodwin v the country (2002), in which the international court of human rights found the country in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the Convention, and reversed Corbett v Corbett (1970), which had barred any change to the sex marker on a birth certificate. Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the national health service or privately, and a December 2002 government policy document states that transsexualism is not a mental illness. Since December 2023 the government no longer accepts gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and sub-national jurisdictions, including one neighbouring jurisdiction and one state/province, on the stated ground that those jurisdictions allow people to transition too easily; affected applicants must apply for a domestic GRC instead. The Women and Equalities Minister called the change long overdue. Under the Gender Recognition Act 2004 as originally enacted, a married transgender applicant had to divorce or annul the marriage before a certificate could be issued. Under current law a GRC will not be issued unless the spouse consents, and if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated. Same-sex marriage has been legal across the country since 2014, with the final region following on 13 January 2020. In For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59 (Outer House, a first-instance division of the regional supreme civil court, 19 June 2026), a judge struck down the regional prison service's non-statutory guidance that had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than sex at birth, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. Earlier in the litigation, on 5 February 2026, the court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, with government lawyers defending individual risk assessments as flexible. The national transport police amended its strip-searching policy after the April 2025 top-court gender ruling, so that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had allowed trans women staff to intimately search women holding a GRC. One state/province police service's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 provides that searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex in custody and stop-and-search, though where lived gender differs an officer of the individual's lived gender will be provided on request. One regional police service's searching and biological-sex policy, released under freedom-of-information law, could not be retrieved at research time. New national equality-body guidance on single-sex spaces came into force on 5 August 2026 as a statutory code of practice, giving organisations practical examples for compliance; one region, on different equality legislation, is still assessing the top-court ruling's impact. On 17 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that the revised code of practice risks discriminating against and excluding transgender people; the warning concerns that statutory code, which is in force, rather than any enacted amendment to the national equality act. An organisation has announced that it is supporting a legal challenge to the code and has backed a pre-action letter; whether proceedings have been filed, their outcome, and how the code will be applied in practice remain unresolved. A regional rainbow-index assessment for 2026 holds that the country maintains explicit bans or other legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible, and provides hate-crime and hate-speech protection on gender identity only in some regions. The national health service said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the health service had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since a national clinical review, with some families turning to black-market or imported hormones instead. The review (April 2024) also led to the closure of the national gender identity service for children in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. A December 2020 court case found children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers, overturned on appeal in September 2021. Trans hospital patients are to be banned from female- and male-only wards under plans announced by the health secretary at an October 2023 party conference, alongside a commitment that a patient's request for intimate care by someone of the same biological sex will be respected and an update to the health service constitution. The national health department announced a consultation on updates to the constitution to ensure privacy, dignity and safety, with the health secretary stating the changes would recognise different biological needs, criticising diversity spending, ordering a reversal of health service website changes and stopping the health service directing staff to declare pronouns to each new patient. A national trans legal clinic documents the death of Joelle, a 27-year-old trans woman with an aggressive lymphoma: after staff at one NHS trust saw she was a trans woman, she was removed from an available cancer ward bed and placed in a side room, where she spent 16 days deteriorating without cancer pain management, and by the time treatment began the delay was unsurvivable. Her mother states the refusal came the day after the health minister announced plans to block trans women from women's wards. The clinic is pursuing an inquest into national obligations and a clinical negligence claim, and notes that if trans people are blocked from appropriate hospital wards this could become policy across the country. A national trans advocacy organisation's Gendered Spaces Report 2025 surveyed trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents and corroborated their fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces. Anti-trans rhetoric in national media has been described as increasing and becoming more vitriolic since 2016 and super-charged since 2018, and a 2019 study found numerous press articles from 2018 and 2019 written to cast trans people as unreasonable and aggressive. Regional rainbow-index rankings show the country falling sharply in the subregion across the 2015, 2020 and 2025 assessments, with concern about a hostile climate on trans rights recorded in 2020 and the decline described as among the steepest drops in the subregion. A national girls' school trust barred admissions for trans girls without a GRC in January 2022, and in July 2022 the national rugby football unions implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are covered by the national equality act.

### SOURCE EVIDENCE
- Broadcast reporting (19 Jun 2026): a judge ruled the regional prison service's guidance — allowing some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than sex at birth — unlawful; sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis.
- Broadcast reporting (5 Feb 2026): a national court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk; a campaign group is challenging the regional prison guidance (only biological females in the women's estate), with government lawyers defending individual risk assessments as flexible.
- Reporting (17 Apr 2025): the transport police amended its strip-searching policy after the national-court gender ruling — trans women to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; prior policy had let trans women staff intimately search women holding a gender-recognition certificate; one campaign group welcomed the change.
- Regional police guidance (25 Jun 2025): interim guidance on searching transgender persons — searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex (custody and stop-and-search); where lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.
- A constitutional-law analysis (16 Jul 2026) of a ruling striking down a regional prison service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance: critiques the judgment, examining the equality statute, prison rules, a 2004 gender-recognition act and the court's human-rights approach.
- Broadcast reporting (Aug 2026): new equality-watchdog guidance on single-sex spaces has come into force — the code gives organisations practical compliance examples; one devolved region, on different equality legislation, is still assessing the national-court ruling's impact.
- An organisation's report (2025): a survey of trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents corroborating their fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces; full report published as a PDF.
- Legal reporting (18 Aug 2026): international human-rights experts warned that revisions to the equality statute risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.
- An international human-rights press release (17 Aug 2026): UN human rights experts warn that the country's revised code of practice on single-sex spaces, in force as of 5 August 2026, risks institutionalising discrimination against transgender and gender-diverse persons.
- A civil-society organisation's announcement: it is supporting a legal challenge to the revised code of practice on single-sex spaces and reports having backed a pre-action letter; whether proceedings have been filed, and any outcome, is not established by this source.
- A county police force's searching policy could not be retrieved at research time (access error); the underlying document is the force's searching/biological-sex policy (released under freedom-of-information rules).
- The regional rainbow-index assessment's 2026 legal gender recognition findings record for the country 'there is no functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition', count it among those with explicit bans or other legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible, and note that although gender recognition certificates are still issued, the 2025 top-court decision ruled that 'sex'-based protection refers to 'biological sex', so that, for the national equality act's purposes, trans men with a GRC are legally treated as 'biological women' and trans women as 'biological men'.
- The country's top court's press summary (16 April 2025) holds unanimously that the terms 'man', 'woman' and 'sex' in the national equality act refer to biological sex; explains that section 9(1) of the 2004 gender-recognition act treats a GRC holder's acquired gender as applying for all purposes while section 9(3) allows that rule to be displaced by other enactments; identifies separate spaces and single sex services, including changing rooms, hostels and medical services, communal accommodation and single sex higher education institutions, among the provisions requiring a biological interpretation; and states that the interpretation does not remove protection from trans people, with or without a GRC, who remain protected from discrimination on the ground of gender reassignment. The summary states that the full judgment is the only authoritative document.
- The country's 2004 gender-recognition act, section 9 (official text): where a full gender recognition certificate is issued, the person's gender becomes for all purposes the acquired gender, so that the person's sex becomes that of a man or a woman; subsection (1) does not affect things done before the certificate is issued but operates for the interpretation of earlier enactments and documents; subsection (3) provides that subsection (1) is subject to provision made by that act or any other enactment or any subordinate legislation, so the 'for all purposes' rule is expressly subject to statutory exceptions.

### SECONDARY / SITUATIONAL FACTORS
The country's trajectory contrasts with neighbouring jurisdictions: a regional rainbow-index ranking places it far lower in the subregion in 2025 than in 2015, a decline described as among the steepest drops in the subregion from 2024. Despite this, 86% of national respondents agreed homosexuality should be accepted in a 2019 poll and 77% supported same-sex marriage in a 2017 poll; the source notes no poll measuring societal acceptance of transgender people specifically. One region operates under different equality legislation and is still assessing the top-court ruling's impact as of August 2026, so single-sex space rules may differ from the rest of the country. Large LGBT communities exist in several major cities, with gay villages and annual pride festivals, though the source does not attribute transgender-specific tolerance levels to those communities.

### AFFECTS RESIDENTS MORE THAN VISITORS
Transgender youth are covered by the national equality act, and discrimination protections for LGBT people have existed since 1999, extended to all areas under that act. A section prohibiting the promotion of homosexuality by schools and local authorities was repealed in 2003. Civil partnerships, available since 5 December 2005, give most but not all rights of marriage and have recognition issues in other countries. Adoption by same-sex couples has been enabled across the country since the mid-2000s, with the final region following in December 2013. Regional anti-gender-discrimination law was held to apply to trans people in a 1996 court case. A November 2021 judicial review against one clinical commissioning group challenged a fertility policy requiring same-sex female couples to complete 12 rounds of private IVF before publicly funded treatment, where heterosexual couples needed only to try to conceive for two years.

### DELIBERATELY NOT COUNTED
One regional police service's searching and biological-sex policy, released under freedom-of-information law, returned HTTP 403 at research time and its contents are unresolved. The UN experts' warning of 17 August 2026 concerns the statutory code of practice in force from 5 August 2026, not enacted amendments to the national equality act. A legal challenge to the code has been announced and is at pre-action stage; whether proceedings have been filed, and their outcome, remain unresolved, as does how the code will be applied in practice. The trans legal clinic's inquest and clinical negligence claim concerning Joelle's death remain unresolved; no outcome is documented. One region's assessment of the top-court ruling's impact under its distinct equality legislation was still ongoing as of August 2026, with no published outcome.

An executive order signed 20 January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary determined at conception or birth, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the national justice department to "correct the misapplication" of a 2020 Supreme Court employment-discrimination ruling. The same order required national agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender," ordered removal of materials it calls gender ideology, rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in national workplaces, prohibited national funding and promotion of gender-identity policies, and rescinded an earlier executive order addressing LGBTQ rights in national prisons. The foreign ministry stopped processing "X"-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth in February 2025; existing "X"-marker passports remain valid until expiration, and new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a foreign ministry policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travelers have reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, leaving some stranded abroad; a national civil-liberties union sued the foreign ministry on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the policy remains challenged in national courts. Entry screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the foreign ministry announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, and its 24 February 2025 cable instructs posts to add the case-note tag — the same text in all cases refused or pending an advisory opinion under the February 2025 executive order. Where there is a discrepancy in an applicant's documents or records, or other evidence casting reasonable doubt on the applicant's sex, the cable instructs officers to refuse the case and request additional evidence; where an applicant is suspected of wilfully misrepresenting sex or purpose of travel, the adjudicating officer should consider whether the misrepresentation is material such that it supports a permanent, lifetime ineligibility finding under the immigration code's fraud ground — a finding that requires all four elements, for which limited waiver possibilities exist, and which is never automatic. Multiple foreign governments responded: by March 2025 at least eight governments in one region, including two named neighbouring jurisdictions, had adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, following detentions of citizens from a neighbouring jurisdiction over visa issues; by April 2025 several governments were issuing advisories about trans people travelling here over identity-document and data rules. Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of state/provinces. The equality map (data as of 7 November 2026) splits these bans into disjoint groups: 9 state/provinces and 1 state/province prohibit facilities consistent with a person's gender identity in all government-owned buildings, including K-12 schools and colleges; 9 other state/provinces cover K-12 schools and at least some government-owned buildings; and 3 state/provinces cover K-12 schools only. In 6 state/provinces these bans apply to at least some private settings, while all other bans currently on the books apply only to government-owned settings. A further 29 state/provinces, 4 state/provinces and the capital district have no such ban in these mapped categories, though the map notes that other state/province laws or policies defining sex may still affect access beyond the laws shown on the map. It flags 4 state/provinces where state law makes such use a criminal offence in certain circumstances; in one of them the statutory trigger is trespass, not automatic arrest: a person, subject to the exemptions in the subsection and excluding the building's own government employees, who willfully enters a restroom or changing facility designated for the opposite sex at a public building and refuses to depart when asked by an employee of the governmental entity with jurisdiction over that building commits the offence of trespass. On 19 March 2025 a transgender student was arrested in a women's restroom at a state/province capitol and charged with trespass; the arrest was reported in April 2025, noting she was handcuffed, and civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under that state/province's bathroom-restriction law. State/province document rules are tightening. In February 2026 one state/province enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups called it a template, and further targeting bills are pending in state/province legislatures. A national equality map sets out which state/provinces still allow gender-marker changes by licence or birth certificate and under what conditions. A national risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 flagged one additional state/province as the latest "Do Not Travel" state/province for trans people, bringing the total to 4 so flagged, and recorded that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while national policies drove nationwide trends. Other national measures in force or in litigation include a military ban executive order, an executive order of 28 January 2025 describing gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," an executive order of 29 January 2025 directing law enforcement to investigate schools promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a trans minor's social transition, including using preferred names or pronouns, a women's sports ban executive order of 5 February 2025, a January 2025 national funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court. Custody and detention carry documented harm. From 2026 the national corrections bureau adopted one state/province's policies mandating what the source describes as conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, removing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender individuals reported denial of care, and the corrections bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying it with statements such as "If you wanna be a man, I'll treat you like a man"; those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement, and many also reported severe sexual abuse. Official hostility extends to advocacy and speech. In December 2025 the national justice department instructed a national law-enforcement agency to establish a cash reward system for information leading to the identification and arrest of individuals in the leadership of domestic terrorist organizations that conspire with others to commit violations of the provisions of law listed in section 2 of the guidance or other offenses against the country; the same memorandum uses the phrase "radical gender ideology" twice — once among the extreme viewpoints it says animate actors "with a willingness to use violence against law-abiding citizenry," and once in a list of political and social agendas attributed to violent extremist groups more generally — and never as a criterion for the reward. In May 2026 the government's counterterrorism strategy stated that national counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is hostile to the country, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide. Marriage recognition stands on a different footing from the document and facilities regimes. Same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under a 2015 Supreme Court ruling, and a December 2022 statute repealed the earlier national marriage-defence act and required all state/provinces to recognize existing same-sex marriages; recognition still varies, with same-sex marriages not licensed or recognized in one outlying state/province and status differing across sovereign tribal nations. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited nationally under a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, and gender-identity hate crimes are punishable under a national hate-crimes statute, though only 23 state/provinces cover gender identity in state/province bias-motivated violence statutes and 37 lacked anti-bias statutes for gender-identity crimes as of 2019. Twenty-two state/provinces plus the capital district outlaw discrimination based on gender identity or expression. Public opinion data from a 2025 poll cited in the sources found 66% of residents supported laws requiring assigned sex at birth to be listed on government documents such as driver's licences and passports (89% of one major party's supporters, 66% of independents, 38% of the other major party's), and 69% supported laws requiring transgender athletes to compete aligned with assigned sex at birth. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 state/provinces, and in October 2025 proposed national health rules would bar public insurance reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18.

### SECONDARY / SITUATIONAL FACTORS

### ASSESSMENT
No criminal provision in the country's law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The legal code derives from the 1889 code of a neighbouring jurisdiction and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender. The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the dominant religious institution and by the country's law. The country has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the country. For a trans visitor, it is unknown whether a trans-specific rule governs access to single-sex facilities, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor. The country operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by the country serves the term in prisons in a neighbouring jurisdiction at the country's expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under the country's authority. A religious education office's 2019 document frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to religious institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity. A 2023 declaration by the doctrinal office permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves. The country has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. The head of the dominant religious institution in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside that institution while maintaining that marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. In 2021 the foreign minister wrote to the ambassador of a neighbouring jurisdiction objecting to a parliamentary bill there meant to protect LGBT people against violence and discrimination. The objection targeted the provision prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which the letter described as a violation of freedom of speech and of religion, and asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated. On 13 January 1998 an activist set himself on fire in a central square, under the country's jurisdiction, in protest at the dominant religion's refusal of homosexuality. He died days later in hospital from severe burns.

Travel documents are the sharpest immediate exposure for a trans visitor to the country. An executive order signed 20 January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary determined at conception or birth, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the national justice department to "correct the misapplication" of a 2020 Supreme Court employment-discrimination ruling. The foreign ministry stopped processing "X"-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth in February 2025; existing "X"-marker passports remain valid until expiration, and new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a foreign ministry policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travelers have reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, leaving some stranded abroad; a national civil-liberties union sued the foreign ministry on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the policy remains challenged in national courts. Entry screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the foreign ministry announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, and its 24 February 2025 cable instructs posts to add the case-note tag — the same text in all cases refused or pending an advisory opinion under the February 2025 executive order. Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of state/provinces. The equality map (data as of 7 November 2026) splits these bans into disjoint groups: 9 state/provinces and 1 state/province prohibit facilities consistent with a person's gender identity in all government-owned buildings, including K-12 schools and colleges; 9 other state/provinces cover K-12 schools and at least some government-owned buildings; and 3 state/provinces cover K-12 schools only.
